title: A zonal instrument view turns one flame video into many small time series, one per height band
summary: The tracked flame edge is cut into horizontal height zones, and the flame width in each zone becomes its own trace. Reading the instrument frames tells you what is measured and when; reading the campaign summaries (RMS and coefficient of variation per zone) tells you where along the flame the fluctuation lives and how repeatable that is across runs.

media.alt: Four instrument panels in a two by two grid, labelled ignition transient, steady laminar, flickering onset and periodic flickering, all for run MVI_8036. Each has a real flame frame on the left with the tracked edge in cyan and eight dashed horizontal zone lines, and four stacked traces on the right: flame height, area, volume and a width-versus-time panel. The traces are flat or empty at ignition, nearly flat in steady laminar, visibly noisy at onset and strongly oscillating in periodic flickering.

source.caption: All four regimes at once -- multi-location width tracking, one frame
source.note: Group explainer for the zonal topic. Six of the eight figures are instrument views (frame plus live traces), usually shown as a video whose still poster is the very first frame, so the traces look empty; two are campaign statistics. Only generic, standard readings are taught here; the tracking algorithm itself is not described.

read_the_figure.question: How wide is the flame at each height, how does that width fluctuate in time, and does the pattern repeat from run to run?
read_the_figure.axes: Instrument frames: left, a real video frame with the tracked flame edge (cyan), the tip marker (red dot) and eight dashed zone lines, z1 at the burner exit up to z8, each 15 mm tall (z1 is 0 to 15 mm, z8 is 105 to 120 mm). Right, four stacked panels sharing a rolling time window of about 18 s: flame height in mm, area in mm squared, volume in mm cubed, and a width panel whose horizontal axis is flame width in mm and whose vertical axis is time in s, running downward, one trace per zone. Campaign statistics: figure 22 has zone mid-height in mm on x and RMS width fluctuation in mm on y, one grey line per run plus a dark ensemble median with a shaded band; figure 23 has the zones z1, z2, z3 on x and the width coefficient of variation on y, one grey dot per run and a dark square for the ensemble median with an interquartile bar.
look_at: Top-left text block (the heads-up display): height, area, tip position, volume and a heat-release number for one frame. In the four quadrants the height reads about 4.9 mm, 60 mm, 109 mm and 94.5 mm: the flame is tiny at ignition, and the numbers are per frame, not averages

The traces in quadrant 2 (steady laminar) are nearly flat lines; in quadrant 3 and 4 the same traces wander and then oscillate. The change in texture of the traces, not their level, is what separates the regimes.
The stacked width traces at the bottom right: where they wobble is where the edge moves sideways. Compare the lower zones (small wobble) with the upper zones (large wobble).
Figure 22: the dark line climbs with height, from roughly 1.8 mm near 22 mm height to about 3 mm near 85 mm and over 4 mm near 115 mm. Grey run lines are spread by about a factor of two between runs.
Figure 23: the median CV rises from about 0.13 (z1) to 0.20 (z2) to 0.52 (z3), and the single dots at z3 sit at about 0.52 and 0.64.
read_the_figure.proves: Together the frames and the zone statistics show that fluctuation intensity depends on height and on regime, and that the same ordering can be recovered in more than one run. That is a statement about the technique and the observed ordering, not a proof of mechanism.
if_wrong: Traces that look empty in a thumbnail: the still image is the first frame of a video, taken before ignition. It is not a failed measurement.
A zone trace with gaps or spikes: the edge was lost in that zone for some frames (for example behind a glare or above the flame tip), so the width there is undefined, not zero.
A very large CV in the top zone: the denominator, mean width, is small and intermittent, so CV inflates. That is a property of the ratio, not necessarily more physical fluctuation.
A median line with kinks that the individual runs do not have: the ensemble median is computed on a sparse, unevenly placed set of zone heights, so it can jump between runs.
must_check: The zone definition and which zones were used for each statistic: the instrument draws eight 15 mm bands, the campaign plots use three named zones. The mapping between them is not on the figures.
The pixel-to-millimetre scale for every run and the time window of each panel.
Whether each dot or line is one run (the legend lists eight run names in figure 22, none in figure 23).
That an interquartile range, not a standard deviation, is the bar in figure 23, and that with eight runs a quartile is determined by only two or three values.
The fraction of frames with a valid edge in each zone.
as_drawn: Values are read by eye from the figures and are approximate, about 10 percent for the plots.

Quadrant HUDs (small type, approximate): ignition height 4.9 mm, area 20 mm squared, volume 114 mm cubed; steady laminar 60 mm, 845 mm squared, about 1.0e4 mm cubed; flickering onset 109 mm, about 1.2e3 mm squared, 1.2e4 mm cubed; periodic flickering 94.5 mm, about 1.1e3 mm squared, 1.1e4 mm cubed.

The HUD heat-release number equals 1e-6 times the volume in mm cubed in all four quadrants (for example 0.0102 against 1.02e4), so in this view it is a rescaled volume, not an independent measurement.
Rolling windows in the four quadrants cover about 143 to 162 s, 294 to 312 s and 478 to 495 s for the last three regimes, and about minus 15 to 0 s for ignition.
Figure 23 median CV: about 0.13, 0.20 and 0.52 for z1, z2, z3.

terms.meaning: A horizontal band of the flame image between two heights above the burner exit. The width of the flame inside the band is measured on every frame.
A display in which a signal scrolls as it is measured, here several signals side by side, so changes in texture are visible at a glance.
Horizontal distance between the left and right detected edge at one height, converted from pixels to millimetres with the run's scale.
Root-mean-square deviation of a signal from its own time mean. For a width signal it equals the standard deviation of w over the window.
The standard deviation divided by the mean, a dimensionless relative spread. It lets a thin zone and a wide zone be compared.
A stretch of the record with its own character: ignition transient, steady laminar, flickering onset, periodic flickering, in that order in this run.
Across runs, the middle value and the range between the 25th and 75th percentile. Robust to one odd run, but coarse when there are only eight.
The block of per-frame numbers drawn on the video frame itself.

remember: A scrolling instrument shows the current frame; a summary figure shows statistics over a window. Do not mix them.
RMS fluctuation of a signal about its mean equals its standard deviation: w'_rms = sqrt(mean((w - mean w)^2)).
CV = standard deviation / mean, so RMS = CV times mean width. A high CV can come from a small mean as easily as a large wobble.
Many small time series (one per zone) show where in space something happens; one number per frame cannot.
A single run is an example; agreement of the ordering across runs is the evidence.
With eight runs an IQR rests on a handful of points: show the points, as figure 23 does.

understand.title: Why zones instead of one width
understand.text: The flame is not one number wide. A laminar flame is narrow and almost steady at the bottom; instabilities grow as the flow moves up, so the same video holds quiet and noisy regions at once. Cutting the edge into height bands keeps that spatial information. The eight dashed lines in the frames are the cuts and each band gets its own trace in the lower right panel.

understand.title: Why four regimes in one frame
understand.text: The 2 by 2 view compares ignition, steady laminar, onset and periodic flickering with identical axes. You can see the signature of each regime in the traces: nothing yet, flat, irregular wobble, and sustained oscillation. The regime names are descriptive labels for this record, not a classification derived on the figure.

understand.title: Why repeat the instrument on other runs
understand.text: The posters for the second and third run show the same layout. A technique that gives the same ordering of regimes on independent footage is more trustworthy than one that was tuned on a single video. From the posters alone you can only confirm that the layout is the same; the traces are in the videos.

understand.title: Reading figure 22 and figure 23 together
understand.text: Figure 22 shows absolute fluctuation (mm), figure 23 relative fluctuation (CV). Both rise with height, so the effect is not only that wider parts of the flame wobble more in absolute terms.

steps.title: One zone, one time series
steps.note: At zone height y_k the width is the right edge position minus the left edge position, in millimetres after scaling. Repeating over frames gives one trace per zone.

steps.title: Mean and RMS fluctuation
steps.note: The RMS is the standard deviation of the width over the analysis window (with the divisor N; the sample version divides by N minus one). Both statistics need a window long enough to contain several flicker periods.

steps.title: The coefficient of variation
steps.note: Dividing by the mean makes the spread dimensionless. If the mean width shrinks while the wobble stays the same, CV rises.

steps.title: Robust summary over runs
steps.note: With eight runs the median is the average of the 4th and 5th ordered values. The interquartile range ignores the two most extreme runs on each side.

steps.title: Why the spread of CV grows when the mean is small
steps.note: First-order propagation for a ratio of independent quantities. In an intermittent top zone the mean width is small and poorly known, so the ratio is poorly known too. This is the standard uncertainty-propagation rule (GUM), applied to the ratio.

worked.title: From CV back to millimetres
worked.problem: Figure 23 gives a median CV of about 0.13 in the lowest zone. Suppose, as an assumption, that the mean width in that zone is 12 mm. What RMS width fluctuation does that imply, and how does it compare with figure 22 near 22 mm height?

solution.text: RMS equals CV times mean width.
Figure 22's ensemble median near 22 mm height is about 1.8 mm, the same order.

worked.answer: About 1.6 mm for the assumed 12 mm mean width: consistent in size with figure 22. The 12 mm is an assumption, not read from the figure, so this is a plausibility check on the two figures, not a measurement.

analyze.q: Figure 22's ensemble median rises sharply between about 113 mm and 117 mm, while the grey run lines are drawn between only two or three points each. How much of that jump reflects flame behaviour and how much reflects which runs contribute at which heights?
analyze.hint: Count how many runs have a point near each height.

analyze.q: The top zone has both the largest RMS and the largest CV. Give two different explanations, one physical and one about the measurement, and say which extra view (frames, edge validity) would separate them.
analyze.hint: Intermittent flame tip, small denominator, edge loss.

analyze.q: The posters for 14, 17 and 18 are essentially empty. What can and cannot be concluded from them about the three runs?
analyze.hint: They are first frames of videos.

evaluate.q: Is eight runs enough to call the rise of CV with height a result? What would you add to the figure so a reader can judge?
evaluate.hint: Per-run values, number of frames, window length, a trend test or at least rank agreement.

evaluate.q: The HUD heat-release number is a constant times volume in all four quadrants. Does a reader need to be told? How should it be labelled?
evaluate.hint: A proxy is fine if it is named as one.

create: Redesign the campaign summary so zone height, mean width and RMS appear together: a dot plot of RMS per zone, annotated with the mean width and the number of valid frames.
Design a check that the zone edges are placed in the same physical heights for every run, and where you would display it.

checks.q: Why does the instrument use eight zones rather than a single width trace?
checks.answer: Because the fluctuation is not uniform along the flame. A single width would average quiet and noisy parts together; one trace per height band keeps the spatial pattern.

checks.q: A zone has mean width 10 mm and CV 0.2. What is its RMS fluctuation?
Zone z3 has CV about 0.52 and z1 about 0.13. Does that prove the flame fluctuates four times more at z3?
checks.hint: Remember what is in the denominator.
checks.answer: No. CV is relative to the mean width, so a smaller or intermittent mean width raises it. The absolute RMS in figure 22 also rises with height, which supports a real increase, but the factor is not four.

checks.q: The ensemble median in figure 22 has kinks. Is it a good summary line?
checks.hint: How many runs contribute at each height?
checks.answer: Only partly. The line is a median over a few unevenly placed points, so it jumps where the contributing runs change. A binned or per-zone median with the number of runs stated would be safer.

checks.q: How would you test that the zonal pattern is a property of the flame and not of one video?
checks.hint: Use independent runs and fixed criteria.
checks.answer: Compute the same per-zone statistics on every run with the zones and scale fixed in advance, show every run, and report the rank agreement of the zone ordering across runs rather than only the median.
